etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English perfeccioun, from Old French perfection, from Latin perfectiō. Displaced native Old English fulfremednes.

definitions.definition: The quality or state of being perfect or complete, so that nothing substandard remains; the highest attainable state or degree of excellence
A quality, endowment, or acquirement completely excellent; an ideal; faultlessness; especially, the divine attribute of complete excellence.

quote.citation: a. 1587, Philippe Sidnei [i.e., Philip Sidney], “(please specify the folio)”, in [Fulke Greville; Matthew Gwinne; John Florio], editors, The Countesse of Pembrokes Arcadia [The New Arcadia], London:  […]  [John Windet] for William Ponsonbie, published 1590, →OCLC:
quote.text: No tongue can her perfections tell

definitions.definition: (now uncommon and nonstandard, transitive) To perfect.

quote.citation: 1762, [Samuel] Foote, The Orators. […], Dublin:  […]  Thomas Richey, […], →OCLC, Act I, page 10:
quote.text: My plan, gentlemen, is to be conſider'd as a ſuperſtructure on that admirable foundation laid by the modern profeſſor of Engliſh, both our labours tending to the ſame general end; the perfectioning of our countrymen in a moſt eſſential article, the right uſe of their native language.

quote.citation: 1770, William Woty, Mock Invocation to Genius‎[1]:
quote.text: Sooner I'd kneel unto the modern nine / Alike perfectioned, though a virgin's name / They cannot boast […]

quote.citation: 2001 December 3, OLF, i.e. Olf Le Fol, “AHSM Storytellers, Profiles”, in alt.hentai.sailor-moon‎[2] (Usenet):
quote.text: The most vain of the Assistants, she knows she's beautiful and let it know to the world. Acts like an ojousama and spends most of her time perfectioning her make-up.
